1.pericope_label: Now as touching things offered unto idols, we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth. And if any man think that he knoweth any thing, he knoweth nothing yet as he ought to know. But if any man love God, the same is known of him.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin open the question and the concession. Gill explains that this was another of the things the Corinthians had written to the apostle about, a controversy that had been moved before: it was considered in the council at Jerusalem, and agreed for the peace of the churches that the Gentiles be advised to abstain from things sacrificed to idols, which it seems the church at Corinth knew nothing of. Some who were weak in the faith and had no clear notion of gospel liberty thought it criminal and sinful to eat them; others who boasted more knowledge would not only eat them privately at home, having bought them of the heathen priests or in the common meat markets where they were exposed to sale, and at public feasts to which they were invited by their friends, but would even go into an idol's temple and sit and eat them there, to the great grief and prejudice of weak Christians. On the second verse Gill glosses the man who thinks he knows as one conceited with his own knowledge who fancies he knows more than he does, which is always the case of those who are elated with knowledge and treat others with contempt without regard to their peace and edification; and on the third, that those love God who love their brethren and are careful not to grieve them, using their superior knowledge not for destruction but edification. Calvin explains that Paul now passes to another question, touched on in the sixth chapter but not fully discussed, of how we ought to restrain our liberty in intermediate things — things neither good nor bad in themselves but indifferent, which God has put in our power, but in the use of which we ought to observe moderation, that there may be a difference between liberty and licentiousness. He selects one instance distinguished above the others, their having been present at the sacred banquets held by idolaters in honour of their gods and eating indiscriminately of the meats offered to them, and teaches that they rashly perverted the liberty granted them by the Lord. He begins with a concession, voluntarily granting everything they were prepared to demand: I see what your pretext is, you make Christian liberty your pretext, and there is not one of you so ignorant as not to know it; I grant all this to be true, but of what avail is that knowledge which is ruinous to the brethren? On the second verse Calvin insists that Paul does not condemn knowledge but the ambition and haughtiness which ungodly men contract in consequence of it; he does not exhort us to be sceptical, so as to be always hesitating and hanging in doubt, and does not approve of a false and counterfeit modesty, as if it were a good thing to think that we are ignorant of what we do know. The beginning of all true knowledge is acquaintance with God, which produces humility and submission and prostrates us entirely instead of elating us; but where pride is, there is ignorance of God. On the third verse he draws the conclusion, that no learning is commendable that is not steeped in love, since that alone secures that our endowments are approved by God; to be known means to be held in any estimation or reckoned among his sons, so that Paul erases all proud persons from the book of life and from the roll of the pious.

Henry supplies the social setting. The case of things offered to idols occurred frequently in that age of Christianity, when the church of Christ was among the heathen and the Israel of God had to live among the Canaanites. It was a custom among the heathen to make feasts on their sacrifices and not only to eat themselves but to invite their friends; these were usually kept in the temple where the sacrifice was offered, and if anything was left when the feast ended it was usual to carry away a portion to friends, while what remained after all belonged to the priests, who sometimes sold it in the markets. Feasts, as Athenæus informs us, were always accounted among the heathen sacred and religious things, so that they were wont to sacrifice before all their feasts, and it was accounted a very profane thing among them to eat at their private tables any meat whereof they had not first sacrificed. In this circumstance of things, while Christians lived among idolaters and had many relations and friends who were such, with whom they must keep up acquaintance and maintain good neighbourhood and therefore had occasion to eat at their tables, what should they do if anything that had been sacrificed were set before them, and what if they were invited to feast with them in their temples? It seems, Henry adds, as if some of the Corinthians had imbibed an opinion that even this might be done, because they knew an idol was nothing in the world.

Barnes, Ellicott, Robertson and Lightfoot handle the case and the wording. Barnes describes the division of a heathen sacrifice, a part given to the officiating priest, a part consumed on the altar, and a part, probably the principal part, the property of him who offered it, which was either eaten at home as food consecrated by having been offered to an idol, or partaken of at a feast in honour of the idol, or in some instances exposed for sale in the market; whether it would be right to partake of that food, either when invited to the house of a heathen friend or when it was exposed for sale, was a question that could not but present itself to a conscientious Christian, the objection being that to partake would be to lend countenance to idolatry, while many supposed it always lawful and the scruples of their brethren needless. On the second verse Barnes takes the sentence to condemn that vain conceit of knowledge or self-confidence which leads a man to despise others or disregard their interests: true knowledge will make us humble, modest and kind, and a man who has not so learned anything as to make it contribute to the happiness of others has never learned the true design of the first elements of knowledge; it is as true now as then that a man may be a miser in knowledge as in wealth, living to accumulate and never to impart. On the third he explains that there is no true and real knowledge which is not connected with love to God, so that a man's course is not to be regulated by mere knowledge however great, and takes the verb known in the sense of approved and loved by God. Ellicott describes the sale of sacrificial meat by the priests, who received a large share for themselves, or by individuals who had more remaining than they could use, so that a Christian might unconsciously eat of meat which had been brought into contact with an idol; some in Corinth felt no scruple, holding that an idol could neither consecrate nor pollute, and would buy without caring whence the meat came, partake of a heathen friend's hospitality, and even join in a repast held in the outer court of a heathen temple, where the meat would almost certainly be what had been saved after the sacrifice. That Paul would have done so himself, Ellicott adds, so far as his own personal feelings alone were concerned, we can scarcely doubt, and it was to him that those who acted on his authority appealed. On the second verse he says there must be a moral as well as a merely intellectual element in knowledge if it is to be true knowledge, since without love to guide us in its use it is not operative and does not fulfil the end of knowledge; and he reports the suggestion that not yet has here the force of not in the infirmities of their mortal state, but judges that such an interpretation introduces altogether a new element of thought to which there is no antithetical explanation in what follows. On the third he says love to God and therefore love to man builds up the whole Christian communion, the man getting outside the merely selfish thought of his own indulgence in his liberty, and finds an under-thought of the identity between knowing God and being known of him, the latter being the source of the former, so that like water rising to its own level the love and the knowledge rise as high as their source. Robertson notes that the Corinthians had plainly asked about this problem in their letter, that the compound adjective for things sacrificed to idols is found only in the New Testament and ecclesiastical writers, and that the connection between idolatry and impurity was very close, especially in Corinth; the word meant the portion of flesh left over after the heathen sacrifices, which the heathen themselves called by another name, and which was either eaten sacrificially, taken home for private meals, or sold in the markets, so that three questions are involved and Paul discusses them all. The clause about all having knowledge he suspects may be a quotation from the letter, and says Paul admits that all Christians have this knowledge since their conversion. On the second verse he notes the article with both knowledge and love, making the contrast sharper, and says love is the solution, not knowledge, in all social problems; the perfect infinitive means to have gone to the bottom of the subject, while the aorist is a summary statement of the man's ignorance, and he cites Newton's remark that he was only gathering pebbles on the shore of the ocean of truth, adding that the really learned man knows his ignorance of what lies beyond, and that shallow knowledge is like the depth of the mud hole, not of the crystal spring. On the third verse he observes that it is not certain whether the pronoun refers to the man who loves God or to God who is loved, and that both are true, since God knows those that are his and those who know God are known of God; the perfect passive marks an abiding state of recognition by God, and no one is acquainted with God who does not love him. Lightfoot holds that the knowledge spoken of is the knowledge of the liberty of the gospel, and that the words are spoken ironically, as if the apostle had said that it is concluded by all that they know that evangelical liberty sufficiently, and thereupon some run out into things which are not convenient; for knowledge puffeth up, renders men bold and neglects the consciences of others, and he that in this sense seems to know something as yet knows nothing as he ought to know.

Clarke and Wesley supply the background and the gloss. Clarke says the whole chapter is better understood in the light of one fact, that there had long subsisted a controversy between the Karaites and the Traditionists over how far it was lawful to derive any benefit or advantage from things used by the Gentiles: the Karaites were a sect of the Jews who scrupulously held to the letter of the sacred writings, taking that alone for their directory, while the Traditionists followed the voice of the elders, interpreting the divine testimonies by their decisions; and from a Karaite work Triglandus has extracted decisions which throw light on the subject, among them that it is unlawful to receive any benefit from any kind of heathen worship or from anything that has been offered to an idol. On the second verse Clarke says the person who acts in this rash, unfeeling way, from the general knowledge he has of the vanity of idolatry and of the liberty the gospel affords from Jewish rites, with all his knowledge does not know this, that though the first and greatest commandment is to love the Lord with all the heart, the second is like unto it, to love one's neighbour as oneself; he then that can torment his neighbour's weak or tender conscience with his food or his conduct does not love him as himself, and therefore knows nothing as he ought to know. On the third he says that to love God in the way the commandment requires will necessarily beget love to one's neighbour, and that such a man is approved of God and acknowledged as his genuine follower. Wesley introduces the chapter as answering the next question they proposed, calls the statement that all of us have knowledge a gentle reproof of their self-conceit, and says that knowledge without love always puffeth up while love alone edifies and builds us up in holiness. On the second verse he adds that a man knows nothing aright unless so far as he is taught by God, seeing there is no true knowledge without divine love; and on the third that he is known, that is, approved, by him.

Chrysostom sets out the situation the chapter addresses. It is necessary first to say what the meaning of the passage is, for he that sees a charge brought against anyone will not understand what is said unless he first perceives the nature of the offence. The charge is a heavy one and the cause of many evils: many among the Corinthians, having learnt that not the things which enter in defile the man but the things which proceed out, and that idols of wood and stone and demons have no power to hurt or help, had made an immoderate use of their perfect knowledge of this to the harm both of others and of themselves. They had gone in where idols were and had partaken of the tables there, producing thereby great and ruinous evil. On the one hand those who still retained the fear of idols and knew not how to contemn them took part in those meals because they saw the more perfect sort doing it, and got the greatest injury, since they did not touch what was set before them with the same mind as the others but as things offered in sacrifice to idols, so that the thing was becoming a way to idolatry. On the other hand these very persons who pretended to be more perfect were injured in no common way, partaking in the tables of demons.

debates: How the opening clause is meant. Lightfoot reads it as irony, that they are all agreed they know the liberty of the gospel well enough; Robertson suspects a quotation from the Corinthians' own letter and lets Paul admit its truth; Calvin makes it a deliberate concession granting everything they demand before asking what such knowledge is worth; Wesley calls it a gentle reproof of self-conceit.

What knowing nothing as one ought means. Calvin denies that knowledge itself is condemned and refuses to let the verse teach scepticism or a counterfeit modesty; Barnes makes the fault a failure to use knowledge for others, a miserliness in knowledge; Clarke turns it on the second commandment and the tormenting of a weak conscience; Robertson makes it a matter of depth, citing Newton on pebbles beside an unexplored ocean; Ellicott reports a rival sense for not yet and rejects it as answering to nothing in the context.

Who is known in the last clause. Barnes, Clarke, Wesley and Calvin all take the verb of divine approval, Calvin adding that the proud are thereby erased from the roll of the pious; Ellicott makes being known of God the source of knowing him; Robertson alone declines to fix the referent, holding that both the man and God may be meant and that both statements are true.

What made the practice a live question. Chrysostom traces the harm to both parties, the weak drawn into idolatry and the strong seated at the tables of demons; Henry and Barnes set out the machinery of sacrifice and market; Ellicott judges that Paul personally would have felt free to eat; Gill recalls the Jerusalem decree that the Corinthians seem not to have known; Clarke sets the whole beside a standing Jewish dispute about benefit from heathen things.
outliers: Clarke alone approaches the chapter through a Jewish controversy rather than a Christian one, setting the Karaites against the Traditionists and quoting a Karaite ruling that no benefit may be taken from anything offered to an idol.

Henry alone appeals to a classical authority for the religious character of heathen dining, citing Athenæus that all their feasts were accounted sacred and that eating unsacrificed meat at a private table was reckoned profane.
themes: if any man think that he knoweth any thing
the same is known of him

4.pericope_label: As concerning therefore the eating of those things that are offered in sacrifice unto idols, we know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is none other God but one. For though there be that are called gods, whether in heaven or in earth, (as there be gods many, and lords many,) But to us there is but one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things, and we by him.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the resumption, the names and the confession. Gill notes that the apostle, having enlarged on the head of knowledge which those who made an ill use of their liberty urged in favour of their conduct, returns to the subject in question in relation to meats; that those called gods are so by name though not by nature, being so called in Scripture, as angels and magistrates, or by men who give them such names; and that in holding one God, Christians and Jews agree with the best and wisest philosophers of the Gentiles, a point clear from the perfections of God, from one first cause of all things, from the government of the world, and from the writings of the Old and New Testament. Who this one God is, he adds, the Gentiles did not know and the Jews are very ignorant of, but Christians know him to be the Father, by which is meant either God essentially considered, the one God, Father, Son and Spirit, called the Father not in relation to any person in the Godhead but in relation to the creatures, so that he is the Father of spirits, the creator of angels and of the souls of men, the God of all flesh and the author of all the mercies the children of men enjoy; or else God personally considered. Calvin holds that Paul now returns to the statement with which he set out and speaks more plainly of the pretext the Corinthians made use of: since the whole evil took its rise from their being pleased with themselves and despising others, he condemns in general that contemptuous knowledge which is not seasoned with love, and now explains what kind of knowledge it was on which they valued themselves — that an idol is an empty figment of the human brain and must be reckoned as nothing, that the consecration gone through in the name of the idol is a foolish imagination of no importance, and that a Christian is therefore not polluted who, without reverence for the idol, eats of things offered to it. This is the sum of the excuse, and Paul does not set it aside as false, for it contains excellent doctrine, but because they abused it. As to the words, Calvin reports that Erasmus reads that an idol has no existence, and prefers the rendering of the old translation, that an idol is nothing, since the argument is that an idol is nothing inasmuch as there is but one God. On the gods that are called such he says they have the name but the reality is wanting, and divides them: those in heaven are the heavenly hosts, as Scripture terms the sun, moon and the other stars, whose title to divine honours Moses overturns by showing that they were created for our use, so that the sun is our servant and the moon our handmaid; those on earth are properly men and women for whom religious worship has been appointed, since, as Pliny observes, those who had deserved well of mankind had their memory consecrated by religion so as to be worshipped as deities — mortal men afterwards exalted to the rank of deities, and more recently Hercules and Romulus and at length the Caesars. On the confession Calvin argues from what is peculiar to God that there is but one: whatever has its origin from what is foreign to itself is not eternal and consequently is not God, and all things have their origin from one Being, who alone therefore is God. When Paul adds that we are in him, Calvin allows that the clause might have another signification, that as we have our beginning from him so we ought to devote our life to him as its end, and that it is used in that sense elsewhere; but here he takes it as meaning that we subsist in God, since it was by him we were once created and by his power that we are preserved.

Henry shows the vanity of idols. The form of expression in the original is elliptical, so that the words may mean that an idol is nothing in the world, or that there is no idol in the world, or that an idol can do nothing in the world; the meaning in general is that heathen idols have no divinity in them, and therefore in the Old Testament they are commonly called lies and vanities, or lying vanities. They are merely imaginary gods, and many of them no better than imaginary beings; they have no power to pollute the creatures of God and thereby render them unfit to be eaten by a child or servant of God, since every creature of God is good if it be received with thanksgiving, and it is not in the power of the vanities of the heathens to change its nature. Heathen idols are not gods, nor to be owned and respected as gods, for there is no other God but one; and Henry notes that the unity of the Godhead is a fundamental principle in Christianity and in all right religion, so that the gods of the heathens must be nothing in the world and have no divinity.

Barnes, Ellicott, Robertson and Lightfoot handle the structure and the words. Barnes explains that the parenthesis closes with the previous verse and the apostle now proceeds to the real question, repeating the question and the admission that all had knowledge; the admission proceeds through these three verses, and in the next he gives the answer, showing that even on the ground of this admission the conclusion would not follow that it was right to partake of food offered in the temple of an idol. On the many gods he says the heathens everywhere worshipped multitudes and gave them the name of gods, some supposed to reside in heaven though they occasionally visited the earth, others reigning particularly over the earth or sea, and others presiding over the inferior regions; this cannot be an admission that they were truly gods and ought to be worshipped, but a declaration that they were esteemed such and that a large number of imaginary beings were thus adored. On the confession he argues that the word Father is not used as applicable to the first person of the Trinity as distinguished from the second, but is applied to God as God, to the Divine nature as such without reference to that distinction, the Father as distinguished from his offspring, the works that owe their origin to him; this is manifest because the apostle does not use the correlative term Son when he comes to speak of the one Lord Jesus Christ, and because the scope of the passage requires it. Ellicott notes that the subject is resumed after the parenthesis, and suggests that in the repetition of the words we have perhaps a characteristic of a letter written by another from the author's dictation, as was the case with this epistle. An idol, he says, is nothing in itself but a piece of wood or metal and really represents nothing, and the word other in the closing phrase was inserted in later manuscripts, probably from a recollection of the words of the first commandment. The next verse he calls a hypothetic argument in which the verb to be is the emphatic word of the supposition: even assuming that there do exist those beings which are called gods — and we have a right to make such a supposition, since Deuteronomy and the Psalms speak of gods and lords of another kind — the difference between the heathen gods many and the lords and gods of whom the Old Testament speaks is that the former are deities and the latter only a casual way of speaking of angels and other spiritual subjects and servants of the one God. On the confession he paraphrases that for us Christians there exists but one God the Father, from whom alone every created thing has come and for, not in, whom alone we exist, and one Lord Jesus Christ through whom all things are created and by whom we Christians are created spiritually: all creation is of the Father through the Son, and all creation is for the Father and likewise for the Son. The words that we are by him must not be regarded as a repetition of part of the previous thought, but as the words by whom are all things express the fact of physical creation, so these attribute our spiritual re-creation as Christians to the same source; and this verse, Ellicott concludes, sweeps away completely any pantheistic conception which might have been thought to be in the previous words. Robertson takes the probable translation to be that no idol is anything in the world, though no copula is expressed, and explains that the idol was a mere picture or symbol of a god, so that if the god has no existence the idol is a non-entity, a thing Gentile Christians had come to know as Jews and Jewish Christians already knew. The clause about many gods he calls a concessive clause assumed to be true for argument's sake, and glosses the participle as so-called or reputed gods, adding that Paul really denied the existence of these so-called gods and held that those who worshipped idols in reality worshipped demons or evil spirits, agents of Satan. On the confession he notes the strong antithesis to the concession, takes the prepositions to make God the source and the goal of the universe and Jesus Christ the intermediate agent in creation, and observes that Paul here calls Jesus Lord and not God, though he does apply that word to him elsewhere. Lightfoot would render the clause as saying that there is no idol in the world, that is, no representation of God, since the word is by the lexicographers a likeness, an image, a sign, a character, a shadow: idols indeed are in the world made of wood, stone, gold and silver, but there is no representation or figure of God, and none can be. He judges that the apostle hitherto puts on the person of those who made no scruple in eating things offered to idols, as though he had said, you say that you know there is no representation of God in the world and that there is only one God, and that therefore those graven images are mere figments of human mistake and the offering of sacrifices to them a mere invention of men, there being nothing sacred and nothing of religion in them.

Clarke and Wesley take the idols and the confession. Clarke reports Lightfoot's rendering, that there is no idol in the world, with the lexical grounds for it, that the word means a likeness, an image, a sign, a character, a shadow, and that images there are of stone, wood and metal but none of these is any representation of the infinite Spirit; he prefers, however, the meaning he had given before, since the expression that an idol is nothing in the world was common in the Old Testament and among the Jews and was understood by them to mean that these are not the true God but nothings and vanity. On the many gods he says there are many images supposed to be representations of divinities, but the divinities are nothing, the figments of mere fancy, and the images have no corresponding realities; whether in heaven or in earth covers the sun, moon, planets, stars, the ocean, rivers and trees, so that there are nominally gods many and lords many. On the confession he takes the Father as him who produced all things, himself uncreated and unoriginated, and renders the clause we for him, all intelligent beings having been created for the purpose of manifesting his glory by receiving and reflecting his wisdom, goodness and truth; the one Lord Jesus is the only visible Governor of the world and the Church, the Creator and Upholder of the universe, and we are by him in that we are brought to the knowledge of the true God by his revelation, since only the only begotten Son can reveal the Father. The gods, Clarke adds, were their divinities or objects of religious worship, while the lords were the rulers of the world, such emperors as were considered next to gods and some of whom were deified; in opposition to the gods Paul places God the Father, the fountain of being, and in opposition to the lords he places Jesus Christ, who made and governs all things. Wesley glosses an idol as a mere nominal god having no divinity, virtue or power, and the gods that are called such as the celestial, terrestrial and infernal deities of the heathen. On the confession he says that the statement that there is but one God is exclusive not of the one Lord, as if he were an inferior deity, but only of the idols to which the one God is opposed; that all things are from the Father by creation, providence and grace, and we for him as the end of all we are and have and do; and that the one Lord is equally the object of divine worship, all things being created, sustained and governed by him, and we by him having access to the Father and all spiritual blessings.

Cyril of Jerusalem expounds the title Lord as the verse applies it to the Son. The Son of God is Lord, he who was born in Bethlehem of Judaea, according to the Angel who said to the shepherds that there is born this day in the city of David Christ the Lord, and of whom an Apostle says elsewhere that the word God sent to the children of Israel, preaching the gospel of peace by Jesus Christ, declares him Lord of all. When he says of all, Cyril insists, except nothing from his Lordship, for whether Angels or Archangels or principalities or powers or any created thing named by the Apostles, all are under the Lordship of the Son. Of Angels he is Lord, as the Gospels show when the Devil departed from him and the Angels came and ministered unto him, for the Scripture does not say they succoured him but that they ministered to him, that is, like servants; and when he was about to be born of a Virgin, Gabriel was then his servant, having received that service as a peculiar dignity.

debates: How the clause about the idol should be rendered. Lightfoot would translate that there is no idol, meaning no representation of God, and supports it from the lexical range of the word; Clarke reports that rendering and prefers the common Old Testament sense, that the heathen gods are nothings and vanities; Calvin rejects Erasmus's an idol has no existence for the older an idol is nothing, since the argument turns on there being but one God; Robertson supplies no copula and argues from the non-existence of the god to the nullity of its symbol; Henry allows all three constructions as grammatically open.

Whose voice speaks in these verses. Lightfoot holds that Paul assumes the person of those who ate without scruple; Barnes reads the whole as an admission running to the next verse, where the answer begins; Calvin agrees that it is their excuse, but insists Paul does not treat it as false, only as abused.

What the many gods and lords are. Gill makes them gods by name and not by nature, as angels and magistrates are so called; Ellicott grants the supposition its own footing from Old Testament usage and distinguishes heathen deities from the scriptural way of speaking about spiritual servants; Robertson denies their existence outright and identifies the objects of idol-worship as demons; Barnes catalogues the heathen pantheon by region; Calvin divides them into the heavenly bodies, which Moses shows were made for our use, and deified men, citing Pliny on the consecration of benefactors.

What the prepositions of the confession assert. Clarke renders the clause we for him, of beings created to manifest God's glory, and Ellicott presses for rather than in; Calvin weighs that sense and prefers to read it of our subsisting in God, preserved by the power that created us; Ellicott further denies that the closing words repeat the earlier ones, taking the first of physical creation and the second of spiritual.
outliers: Calvin alone explains the deified gods on earth historically rather than theologically, following Pliny in tracing them to benefactors whose memory was consecrated, down to the Caesars.

Cyril of Jerusalem alone treats the title Lord in this verse as a doctrinal proof rather than as a contrast with the lords many, pressing the words Lord of all until nothing created is left outside the Son's dominion.
themes: an idol is nothing in the world
whether in heaven or in earth

7.pericope_label: Howbeit there is not in every man that knowledge: for some with conscience of the idol unto this hour eat it as a thing offered unto an idol; and their conscience being weak is defiled. But meat commendeth us not to God: for neither, if we eat, are we the better; neither, if we eat not, are we the worse.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the limitation and the plea. Gill notes that the apostle is not speaking of heathens, in whom there was no knowledge of the one true God the author of all things, and of the one Lord Jesus the only Saviour, but of Christians, in whom there was the knowledge of these things but not in all of them: though they knew that an idol was not God and had no true deity in it, nor was any true representation of God, they yet fancied that it had an influence upon food offered to it, to defile it and render it unclean, so that it ought not to be eaten; and since there were such persons, so ignorant and weak, it became those who had more knowledge to be careful how they laid stumblingblocks in their way. On the next verse Gill says the words are spoken either as expressing the argument of such as had knowledge in their own favour, that the thing was indifferent, by which they were made neither better nor worse, so that they were not to be blamed for using their liberty; or else as the apostle's own sense, that eating any sort of meat, and so that offered to idols, or abstinence from it, recommends none to the love and favour of God, the phrase meaning, as the Syriac renders it, that it does not bring near or give access to God, nor ingratiate any into his affectionate regards. Calvin holds that Paul refutes in a single word all that he had previously brought forward in their name, showing that it is not enough that they know what they do is right if they have not at the same time a regard to their brethren; having earlier reproved those who abused their liberty, he now calls them to consider that many weak and ignorant persons are associated with them, to whom they ought to accommodate themselves. You have, he says in their hearing, a correct judgment in the sight of God, and if you were alone in the world it would be as lawful for you to eat of things offered to idols as of any other food; but consider your brethren, to whom you are debtors: you have knowledge, they are ignorant, and your actions ought to be regulated not merely according to your knowledge but also according to their ignorance. This reply Calvin thinks particularly deserving of notice, since there is nothing to which we are more prone than that every one should follow his own advantage to the neglect of others, resting in our own judgment and not considering that the propriety of what we do in the sight of men depends on more than that. On the next verse he says this was, or may have been, another pretext of the Corinthians, that the worship of God does not consist in meats, as Paul himself teaches to the Romans; and Paul answers that we must at the same time take care that our liberty does not injure our neighbours. In this he tacitly acknowledges that in the sight of God it matters not what kinds of food we partake of, since he allows us the free use of them so far as conscience is concerned, but that this liberty in its external use is made subject to love; the argument of the Corinthians was therefore defective, inasmuch as they inferred the whole from a part, for a regard to the claims of love is included in the use of them. Calvin adds that Paul does not speak of improvement as to the stomach, for the man who has dined has a better filled stomach than the man who goes fasting, but means that we have neither more nor less of righteousness from eating or from abstaining; nor does he speak of every kind of abstinence or of every kind of eating, for excess and luxury are in themselves displeasing to God, while sobriety and moderation are well-pleasing to him.

Henry marks the turn in the argument. The apostle, having granted and indeed confirmed the opinion of some among the Corinthians that idols were nothing, proceeds to show them that their inference from this assumption was not just, namely that they might therefore go into the idol-temple and eat of the sacrifices and feast there with their heathen neighbours. He does not so much insist on the unlawfulness of the thing in itself as on the mischief such freedom might do to weaker Christians who had not the same measure of knowledge as these pretenders. He informs them that every Christian at that time was not so fully convinced that an idol was nothing, since some, with conscience of the idol, that is with some confused veneration for it, ate it as a thing offered to an idol; though they were converts to Christianity and professed the true religion, they were not perfectly cured of the old leaven but retained an unaccountable respect for the idols they had worshipped before. Weak Christians, Henry observes, may be ignorant, or have but a confused knowledge of the greatest and plainest truths, such as those of the one God and one Mediator; and yet some of those turned from heathenism to Christianity among the Corinthians seem to have retained a veneration for their idols utterly irreconcilable with those great principles.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson handle the exception and the text. Barnes explains that in the previous verses Paul had stated the argument of the Corinthians, that they all knew an idol was nothing, that they worshipped but one God, and that there could be no danger of falling into idolatry even if they partook of meat offered in sacrifice; here he replies that though this might be generally true it was not universally, for some were ignorant on the subject and supposed that an idol had a real existence, so that to partake would confirm them in their superstition, and the inference is that on their account the others should abstain. Some, he says, are weak and ignorant and have still remains of heathen opinions and superstitious feelings; with conscience of the idol means from a conscientious regard to it, believing that an idol god has a real existence whose favour should be sought and whose wrath deprecated. It is not to be supposed that converted men would regard idols as the only God, but they might suppose them to be intermediate beings, good or bad angels, and think it proper to seek their favour or avert their wrath, since the heathen were exceedingly ignorant and their former notions about the gods their fathers worshipped were not easily laid aside. On the next verse Barnes regards the statement as the view presented by the Corinthian Christians or by the advocates for partaking: religion is of a deeper and more spiritual nature than a mere regard to such circumstances, God looks at the heart, and the mere circumstance of eating or abstaining cannot make a man better or worse in the sight of a holy God, from which they inferred that it could not be a matter of much importance whether a man ate the meat or abstained. To this argument, Barnes says, the apostle replies in the verses following, that although it might be true in itself it might be the occasion of leading others into sin and would then become a matter of great importance. The word rendered commendeth means properly to introduce to the favour of any one, as a king or ruler, and here to recommend to the favour of God, which God does not make depend on unimportant circumstances like this. Ellicott says the Apostle had admitted that in theory all have knowledge which should render the eating a matter beyond question, but that there are some who as a matter of fact are not fully grown and have not practically attained it. He would render the next clause: some, through their familiarity with the idol, even up to this time eat it as offered to an idol; the weight of manuscript evidence is in favour of the word familiarity instead of the word conscience, and joins even up to this time not with eat but with the previous words. The allusion is thus to heathen converts who, from their previous lifelong belief in the reality of the idol as representing a god, have not been able fully to realise the non-existence of the person thus represented, though they have come to believe that it is not God, and therefore regard the meat as offered to some kind of reality even though it be a demon; the Apostle admits that this is a sign of a weak conscience, and the defilement arises from its being weak. On the next verse Ellicott says that by showing the eating to be a matter of indifference the Apostle introduces his reason for yielding to the weakness of another, since if the weakness involved a matter of our vital relation to God then to yield would be wrong; but meat will not affect our relationship to God. He notes that the concluding words of the verse are inverted in later manuscripts, as in the English version, and that the better order is: neither, if we eat not, do we lose anything in our relation to God, nor, if we eat, do we gain anything in our relation to him. Robertson glosses the opening as saying that in all men there is not the knowledge of which Paul is speaking, since knowledge has to overcome inheritance and environment, prejudice, fear and many other hindrances. The word he reads is an old one meaning being accustomed to, intimacy, so that it is the force of habit that still grips them when they eat such meat: they eat it as an idol sacrifice though they no longer believe in idols, the idol-taint clinging in their minds to the meat. On the defilement he quotes the judgment that it is defiled not by the partaking of polluted food, for food cannot pollute, but by the doing of something which the unenlightened conscience does not allow; even if unenlightened, one must act according to his conscience, a sensitive gauge of one's spiritual condition, and knowledge breaks down as a guide with the weak or unenlightened conscience. On the next verse he says food will not give us an entree to God for commendation or condemnation, whether meat-eaters or vegetarians, glosses the two verbs as being left behind or falling short and as overflowing or having excess of credit, and observes that Paul here disposes of the pride of knowledge and the pride of prejudice, each party being disposed to look down upon the other, the one in scorn of the other's ignorance and the other in horror of the other's daring.

Clarke and Wesley take the weak conscience and the indifference. Clarke says this is spoken in reference to what was said above, that an idol is nothing in the world; for some, with a conscience of the idol, that is that it is something, eat the flesh offered to it as a thing thus offered, considering the feast as a sacred banquet by which they have fellowship with the idol, and their conscience, being weak and not properly instructed in divine things, is defiled, since the man performs what he does as an act of religious worship and thus contracts guilt through this idolatry. As at the commencement of Christianity many converted Jews were found who incorporated the rites of the law with the principles of the Gospel, so doubtless among the Gentiles there were several who did not at once throw aside all their idolatrous notions but preserved some of the more spiritual and imposing parts, and might think it necessary to mingle idolatrous feasts with the rites of Christianity, the sacrament of the Lord's supper being certainly considered as a feast upon a sacrifice; and since the minds of many of these young Gentile converts could not as yet have been deeply endued with spiritual knowledge, they might incorporate these feasts and confound their nature and properties. On the next verse Clarke says no such feasts as these can be a recommendation of our souls or persons to the Supreme Being, since as to the thing considered in itself the eating gives us no spiritual advantage and the not eating no spiritual loss. Wesley glosses the eating with consciousness of the idol as fancying it is something and that it makes the meat unlawful to be eaten, and the weak conscience as one not rightly informed, which contracts guilt by doing it; and on the next verse he says that meat commends us not to God neither by eating nor by refraining from it, eating and not eating being in themselves things merely indifferent.

debates: What the weak lacked, and what the text says they had. Ellicott reports that the manuscripts favour familiarity rather than conscience, and describes converts who cannot shake the reality of what the idol represented; Robertson reads the same word and makes it the force of habit, the idol-taint clinging in the mind; Henry keeps the received word and glosses it as a confused veneration; Barnes supposes they took idols for intermediate beings whose favour was worth seeking; Gill has them deny the idol's deity while still fearing its power to defile food; Clarke makes the man treat the feast as a banquet giving fellowship with the idol.

How the weak conscience is defiled. Clarke and Wesley make the defilement guilt contracted by an act of religious worship offered to an idol; Robertson, on the contrary, denies that food can pollute at all and locates the defilement in acting against what the conscience, however unenlightened, forbids; Ellicott says only that the defilement arises from the weakness itself.

Whose argument the second verse states. Barnes takes it for the plea of those who wished to partake, answered in the verses that follow; Gill allows that it may be either their argument or the apostle's own sense; Calvin calls it another of their pretexts and faults it for inferring the whole from a part; Ellicott makes it Paul's own premise, the indifference of eating being what allows him to yield to another's weakness.

How far the indifference extends. Clarke, Wesley and Robertson state it flatly, that eating and abstaining give neither advantage nor loss before God; Calvin guards it, that Paul speaks not of the stomach but of righteousness, and not of every kind of eating, since excess and luxury displease God while sobriety pleases him; Ellicott notes that the later manuscripts invert the two clauses that state it.
outliers: Ellicott alone rests his whole reading of the verse on a variant, preferring familiarity to conscience and repunctuating the clause accordingly, so that the weak are described by their habits rather than by their scruples.

Calvin alone refuses to let the indifference of food stand as a general principle, insisting that the verse says nothing about gluttony or abstinence as such, but only that neither eating nor abstaining adds to or subtracts from righteousness.
themes: there is not in every man that knowledge
a thing offered unto an idol
meat commendeth us not to God
if we eat, are we the better
if we eat not, are we the worse

9.pericope_label: But take heed lest by any means this liberty of yours become a stumblingblock to them that are weak. For if any man see thee which hast knowledge sit at meat in the idol's temple, shall not the conscience of him which is weak be emboldened to eat those things which are offered to idols; And through thy knowledge shall the weak brother perish, for whom Christ died?

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the caution and the principle. Gill says the caution is either a reply to those who argued in favour of eating things offered to idols, or a limitation and explanation of the apostle's own concession that the thing made a man, with respect to the favour of God, neither better nor worse. He notes that the man who sees is not any person whatever, nor one of equal knowledge who could take the same liberty with a good conscience, but one weak in the faith who has no clear sight of the doctrine of Christian liberty, and who observes a man famous for superior abilities, learning and knowledge; and he calls the following words an aggravation of the sin of those who by their example ensnare weak minds and cause them to stumble and fall. Calvin holds that Paul leaves their liberty untouched but moderates the use of it so far that it may not give occasion of stumbling to the weak, and expressly desires that regard be had to the weak, that is, to those not yet thoroughly confirmed in the doctrine of piety, since it is the will and command of the Lord that regard should be had to those who are commonly regarded with contempt. In the meantime, Calvin adds, strong giants who may desire tyrannically to subject our liberty to their humour may safely be let alone, because we need not fear giving offence to those who are not drawn into sin through infirmity but eagerly catch at something to find fault with. On the temple feast he observes how much liberty the Corinthians allowed themselves, since when the wicked made a kind of sacred banquet for their idols they did not hesitate to go to it and eat of the sacrifice along with them; and he renders the clauses as a concession, as if Paul had said, be it so that thou hast knowledge, yet he who sees thee, though not endowed with knowledge, is confirmed by thine example to venture upon the same thing, while he would never have taken such a step had he not had one to take the lead, and now that he has one to imitate he thinks he has a sufficient excuse in imitating another, while all the time he is acting from an evil conscience. On the last verse Calvin marks how serious an evil it is, which mankind commonly think so little of, to venture upon anything with a doubtful or opposing conscience: the object to which our whole life ought to be directed is the will of the Lord, and this is the one thing that vitiates all our actions when we disregard it, which we do not merely by an outward action but even by a thought of the mind, whenever we allow ourselves in anything in opposition to conscience, though the thing be not evil in itself; whenever we take a step in opposition to conscience we are on the high road to ruin. He adds that he reads the sentence interrogatively, as though Paul had said, is it reasonable that thy knowledge should give occasion of ruin to thy brother, and is it for this that thou knowest what is right, that thou mayest cause another's ruin?

Barnes, Ellicott, Robertson and Lightfoot supply the argument and the background. Barnes reads the verse as Paul's reply to the argument of the previous one: though all they say should be admitted, and a man is neither morally better nor worse for partaking or abstaining, the grand principle to be observed is so to act as not to injure the brethren, and if their conduct should injure others and lead them into sin that is a sufficient guide, so that they should abstain entirely, it being of far more importance that a brother should not be led into sin than that they should partake of meat which they themselves acknowledge to be of no importance. He calls this a general principle that is to regulate Christian conduct in all matters indifferent in themselves. On the temple he explains that feasts were often celebrated in honour of idols, either in the temple of the idol or at the house of him who gave it, and that the man of knowledge will be looked up to as an example and presumed to be partaking in honour of the idol, so encouraging the weaker to partake with a conscientious regard to it; the word rendered emboldened means confirmed or established, as edify is commonly used in the New Testament. On the last verse he holds that the weak brother means a real Christian, both because brother is the usual term of endearment by which Christians are designated and because the scope of the passage requires it, and that the word perish properly and usually means destroyed or ruined, the sense being that the tendency of this course would be to lead a weak brother into sin, apostasy and ruin; but he denies that this proves that any truly converted should apostatise and be lost, since there may be a tendency to a thing and yet the thing never happen, the event being arrested. Ellicott argues that on this very account, because the matter is indifferent and there is no right or wrong in it, they must look elsewhere for their guide: in things not indifferent right or wrong is the sole test of action, while in things indifferent they must regulate their conduct by the effect it may have on others, since a liberty arising from the bare indifference of the thing may become a stumbling-block and the cause of another's taking a false step in the Christian course. He notes that the fact of being avowedly advanced in the knowledge of the faith makes the example the more dangerous because more effective, that some went so far as not only to eat but to eat in the precincts of the heathen temple, and that the Apostle, being concerned here only with the eating, does not rebuke that practice until a later chapter, mentioning it here as a case in which there could be no salving of conscience by supposing the origin of the meat uncertain. The word emboldened he would render built up, and observes that the people addressed had probably argued that the force of their example would build others up: yes, says the Apostle with irony, it will build him up, to do what, being weak, he cannot do without sin. On the last verse Ellicott holds that it is not, as in the English version, a question, but the expansion and interpretation of the previous statement, and would render it, and by means of thy knowledge the weak one perishes, the brother for whom Christ died; there is a great variety of readings in the manuscripts, but the weight of evidence is in favour of this. The sarcasm, he says, passes away into words of solemn and pathetic reproof: you will not give up your liberty for him, you will indulge yourself and so prevent Christ's death being his redemption, since a sacrifice of conscience destroys spiritual life. Robertson calls the opening a warning to the enlightened, and traces the word rendered liberty through its range of grant, allowance, authority, power, privilege, right and liberty, noting how easily it shades off and how personal liberty becomes a battle cry to those who wish to indulge their own whims and appetites regardless of the effect upon others; the stumbling-block is an obstacle for the foot to strike, and the principle applies to all social relations in matters of law, of health and of morals, the enlightened being bound to consider the welfare of the unenlightened or he does not have love. He draws the picture of the enlightened brother exercising his liberty by eating in the idol's temple, says the peril to the man's own soul is discussed later while here only the effect on the weak brother is considered, and calls such bravado at a sacrificial banquet idolatrous in itself; the weak brother will be built up to go on and do what he still believes to be wrong, which Robertson says has often happened, defiance being flung in the face of the unenlightened brother instead of loving consideration. On the last verse he glosses the phrase as in thy knowledge, calls it a poor use to put one's superior knowledge to, and notes that the appeal to the death of Christ is the central fact that clinches Paul's argument, since Christ died for the weak brother just as much as for the enlightened one with his selfish pride. Lightfoot sets the temple meal beside passages of the Talmudists, where Rabba and Abai dispute whether a man who adores an idol out of love or fear is free or guilty, and the case is resolved by his intention: if he takes the image for God he is guilty, and if not, it is nothing at all; and if he supposes the idol-temple to be the synagogue and adores there, his heart is towards God.

Clarke and Wesley press the danger and the cost. Clarke warns that by frequenting such feasts under the conviction that an idol is nothing, this liberty may become a means of grievously offending a weak brother who has not that knowledge, or of inducing one who respects the eater for his superior knowledge to partake with the persuasion and belief that an idol is something, concluding that as the stronger partakes so may he; the weak man is not possessed of the superior information, and he eats to the idol what the other takes as a common meal. On the temple Clarke asks whether it is not strange that any professing the knowledge of the true God should even enter one of those temples, and more surprising that any Christian should be found to feast there, by which we may see that the boasted knowledge of the Corinthians had very little depth in things purely spiritual; there are many curious thin-spun theories in the rabbinical writings concerning entering idol temples and eating there and even worshipping there, provided the mind be towards the true God, for which he cites Lightfoot, and he suspects the man of knowledge here may have been one of those who, possessing a convenient conscience, could accommodate themselves to all circumstances, being heathen without and Christian within as occasion required. The word emboldened he renders built up, that is confirmed and established in an opinion which before he doubtingly held. On the last verse Clarke says the weak brother, being first taught by the other's conduct that there was no harm in thus eating, grieves the Spirit of God, becomes again darkened and hardened, and, sliding back into idolatry, dies in it and so finally perishes; from which he concludes that a man may perish for whom Christ died, and says this admits of no quibble, since if a man for whom Christ died apostatises from Christianity and returns to and dies in idolatry he cannot go to heaven. Wesley glosses the man of knowledge as one whom the weaker believes to have more knowledge than himself and who really has this knowledge, that an idol is nothing, sitting down to an entertainment in an idol temple, the heathens having frequently made entertainments in their temples on what had been sacrificed; the weak or scrupulous man is encouraged by that example to eat, though with a doubting conscience. On the last verse Wesley observes that Christ died even for them that perish, and that for this brother the strong will not lose a meal's meat, so far are they from dying for him.

debates: Whether the last verse is a question. Ellicott denies it outright, holding against the English version that the words expand the preceding statement and should be read as a declaration that the weak one perishes; Calvin says expressly that he reads the sentence interrogatively, asking whether it is reasonable that knowledge should occasion a brother's ruin.

Whether the perishing is a real possibility. Clarke says it admits of no quibble, since a man who apostatises and dies in idolatry cannot go to heaven; Wesley agrees that Christ died even for them that perish; Barnes grants that a real Christian is meant and that ruin is the tendency of the course, but denies that a tendency proves the event, since it may be arrested.

What the weak brother is built up to do. Barnes and Clarke take the verb as confirming a man in an opinion he had held doubtfully; Ellicott hears irony, the strong having claimed that their example would build others up; Calvin describes the excuse the imitator makes for himself while acting from an evil conscience; Robertson calls the whole a defiance flung at a brother in place of loving consideration.

Who is owed this forbearance. Calvin restricts it to the weak and exempts the censorious, holding that those who catch at faults rather than stumble through infirmity may be let alone; Ellicott and Barnes state the duty generally, as the rule governing all indifferent things; Robertson extends it to all social relations in matters of law, health and morals.
outliers: Clarke and Lightfoot together supply the rabbinic background, Clarke naming Lightfoot as his authority for the thin-spun theories that permitted entering and even worshipping in an idol temple provided the mind were towards the true God, and Lightfoot furnishing the Talmudic disputes themselves.
Calvin alone carves out an exception to the duty of forbearance, refusing it to those who use another's liberty as an occasion of fault-finding rather than being genuinely wounded by it.
themes: a stumblingblock to them that are weak
sit at meat in the idol’s temple
the conscience of him which is weak
things which are offered to idols

12.pericope_label: But when ye sin so against the brethren, and wound their weak conscience, ye sin against Christ. Wherefore, if meat make my brother to offend, I will eat no flesh while the world standeth, lest I make my brother to offend.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin state the offence and the conclusion. Gill explains that the sin against the brethren is committed through sitting at meat in an idol's temple, and thereby violating the new commandment of love, by which saints are obliged to love one another as brethren and to take care to do nothing that may hurt or prejudice one another's peace and comfort, it being an incumbent duty upon them by love to serve one another. On the last verse he calls it the conclusion of the whole, which the apostle makes with respect to himself and proposes for the imitation of others: since an imprudent use of Christian liberty in this article might lay a stumblingblock in the way of weak Christians and embolden them to do things contrary to their consciences, breaking the peace of their minds, wounding their spirits and grieving their souls, and since so to do would be to sin against Christ himself, the apostle determines, in the strength of divine grace, rather than do any of these things or be accessory to them, upon the course he states. Calvin argues that if the soul of every one that is weak is the price of Christ's blood, that man who for the sake of a very small portion of meat hurries back again to death the brother who has been redeemed by Christ shows how contemptible the blood of Christ is in his view, so that contempt of this kind is an open insult to Christ; and he recalls that the way in which a weak conscience may be wounded has already been explained, namely when it is emboldened in what is evil so as daringly and rashly to rush on farther than the individual thinks to be lawful for him. On the last verse Calvin says that, with the view of reproving more severely their disdainful liberty, Paul declares that we ought not merely to refrain from a single banquet rather than injure a brother, but ought to give up the eating of meats during our whole life; nor does he merely prescribe what ought to be done, but declares that he would himself act in this way. The expression is hyperbolical, Calvin allows, since it is scarcely possible that one should refrain from eating flesh during his whole life if he remains in common life; but the meaning is that he would rather make no use of his liberty in any instance than be a stumbling-block to the weak, for participation is in no case lawful unless it be regulated by the rule of love. Would that this were duly pondered, Calvin adds, by those who make everything subservient to their own advantage, so that they cannot endure to give up so much as a hair's breadth of their own right for the sake of their brethren, and that they would attend not merely to what Paul teaches but also to what he marks out by his own example; how greatly superior he is to us, and when he makes no hesitation in subjecting himself thus far to his brethren, which of us would not submit to the same condition?

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson explain the wounding and the resolve. Barnes says the word sin is here to be taken in the sense of injuring, offending, or leading into sin: they violate the law which requires them to love their brethren and seek their welfare, and thus sin against them, for although sin is properly against God there may be a course of injury pursued against men. The word wound he takes in the sense of injure, the consciences being ill-informed and the weak led further into error, believing that the idol is something and is to be honoured, so that they are led into sin and their conscience more and more perverted and oppressed with a sense of guilt. They sin against Christ because he has commanded them to love the weak and seek their good and not to lead them into sin, and because the weak are so intimately united to Christ that to offend them is to offend him, to injure the members is to injure the Head. On the last verse Barnes says Paul proposes his own views and feelings in order to show them how they should act: to make a brother offend means to be the occasion of leading him into error and guilt, not to irritate him; the apostle's own eating is a matter of comparative unimportance which he can dispense with, and is of much less importance to him than happiness, a good conscience and salvation are to his brother, so that the law of love requires him to deny himself rather than be the occasion of leading his brother into sin. Barnes calls this a noble resolution, marking a great, disinterested and magnanimous spirit, one that seeks the good of all and can deny itself, supremely anxious for the glory of God and the salvation of man, and able to make personal comfort subservient to the good of others; it was the principle on which Paul always acted, and is the very spirit of the self-denying Son of God. The phrase rendered while the world standeth he glosses as meaning for ever, so that the words I will never eat meat would express the idea. Ellicott paraphrases the first verse: when you sin in this way, and he explains further what the sin is, striking a blow upon their weak consciences, you sin against Christ, since you wound a member of that body which is his. Robertson notes that the verb rendered wound is an old word for smiting with fist, staff or whip, and that the conscience is sensitive to a blow like that, a slap in the face; the fact that they sin against Christ was what they were overlooking, and he recalls that Jesus had said to Saul that he was persecuting him when he persecuted his disciples, and wonders whether Paul knew the words of Jesus that what was done to the least was done to him. On the last verse Robertson observes that the first word should be food rather than flesh, while the second is flesh with direct reference to the flesh offered to idols; the verb rendered make to stumble is a late word meaning to set a trap-stick or stumbling-block, and small boys sometimes set snares for other boys and not merely for animals, to see them caught. The strong double negative with the second aorist subjunctive gives the force of the resolve, and Robertson concludes that this is Paul's principle of love applied to the matter of eating meats offered to idols, since Paul had rather be a vegetarian than lead his weak brother to do what he considered sin; there are many questions of casuistry today, he adds, that can only be handled wisely by Paul's ideal of love.

Clarke and Wesley press the warning home. Clarke says the sin is against Christians who are called by the Gospel to abhor and detest all such abominations, and that they sin against Christ by sending to perdition, through their bad example, a soul for whom he shed his blood, and so far defeating the gracious intentions of his sacrificial death; this, he adds, is a further intimation that a person for whom Christ died may perish, and is the drift of the apostle's argument. On the last verse he paraphrases the resolve: rather than give any occasion to a Christian to sin, and so to harden his conscience that he should return to idolatry and perish, he would not only abstain from all meats offered to idols but would eat no flesh should he exist through the whole course of time, and would live on the herbs of the field rather than cause his brother to stumble and thus fall into idolatry and final ruin. Clarke then quotes Origen as containing a very solemn lesson and warning, that if we did more diligently attend to these things we should avoid sinning against our brethren and wounding their weak conscience, that we might not sin against Christ, since our brethren for whom Christ died often perish not only by our knowledge but by many other ways and things, in which things we, sinning against Christ, shall suffer punishment, the souls of them that perish by us being required of and avenged upon us. He draws two lessons: that the greater our reputation for knowledge and sanctity the greater mischief we shall do by our influence and example if we turn aside from the holy commandment delivered to us, so that every man should walk so as either to light or lead his brother to heaven; and that it is the duty of every Christian to watch against apostasy in his own case and to prevent it as much as possible in that of others. Wesley glosses the meat as of any kind, and closes with two questions: who will follow this example, and what preacher or private Christian will abstain from anything lawful in itself when it offends a weak brother?

debates: Why an injury to a brother reaches Christ. Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson all argue from union, that the weak are members of the body whose head is Christ, Robertson supporting it from the words spoken to Saul about persecuting Christ; Calvin argues instead from price, that a soul bought with Christ's blood and sold again for a portion of meat shows what that blood is worth in the eater's eyes; Clarke combines the two and adds that the verse intimates a man for whom Christ died may perish.

Whether the closing resolve is to be taken literally. Calvin alone calls the expression hyperbolical, since a man living in common life could scarcely keep it, and reduces the meaning to a willingness to forgo liberty in any instance; Barnes takes the phrase as simply meaning for ever; Robertson takes it at face value and says Paul would rather be a vegetarian; Clarke has him living on the herbs of the field.

What the wounding consists in. Robertson makes it a physical blow, the verb being used of smiting with fist or staff; Barnes makes it the deepening perversion of an ill-informed conscience under a sense of guilt; Calvin makes it the emboldening of a man to go further than he himself thinks lawful; Gill makes it the breach of the commandment of mutual love.

What the reader is to do with the example. Calvin turns it against those who will not yield a hair's breadth of their right and bids them look at what Paul does rather than only at what he teaches; Wesley asks bluntly who will follow it; Clarke quotes Origen that the souls of those who perish by us will be required of us; Robertson applies it to modern questions of casuistry; Barnes holds it up as the spirit of the self-denying Son of God.
outliers: Calvin alone declines to take the closing vow at its face value, calling it a hyperbole and locating its force in the willingness it expresses rather than in the abstinence it promises.

Clarke alone brings a patristic voice into the chapter, citing Origen that those who perish through our example will be required at our hands, and turning the verse into a rule about the danger of a great reputation.
themes: when ye sin so against the brethren
if meat make my brother to offend
lest I make my brother to offend
